lessons.title: Address spaces and why virtual memory exists
lessons.summary: Physical versus virtual addresses, what an address space gives each process, and the historical base-and-bounds and segmentation schemes that paging replaced.
lessons.body:
Run two copies of the same program and print the address of a global variable in each. With a non-PIE executable, disabled address randomization, or a parent/child created by `fork`, the address can match while each process has its own value. Independent ASLR-enabled PIE executions generally choose different layouts. Both statements are true because the address the program sees is not where the data actually lives in RAM.

That illusion is **virtual memory**. Every process gets its own private **address space**: a huge, clean range of addresses that looks as if it belongs to that process alone. The operating system and the hardware quietly map those addresses onto real memory.

This lesson explains why that illusion is worth the effort, and walks through the early hardware schemes (base and bounds, then segmentation) that led to paging, which the rest of the module covers.

## Physical and virtual addresses

A **physical address** identifies a location in the machine's physical address space, which can include RAM, device mappings and holes. 16 GiB contains 2^34 bytes, but installed RAM need not occupy the contiguous range 0 through 2^34−1.

A **virtual address** is what a program uses: every pointer in C, every instruction fetch, every stack push. With four-level x86-64 paging, the lower canonical half spans 2^47 bytes (128 TiB); five-level paging expands it to 2^56 bytes (64 PiB). Actual usable mappings are constrained by kernel policy and reserved regions.

On every single memory access, a piece of hardware in the CPU called the **memory management unit (MMU)** translates the virtual address into a physical one, using tables the OS set up.

```
 process A          MMU           RAM
 0x4000 ----+                +---------+
            +--> translate ->| frame 7 |
 process B  |    (A's map)   |  ...    |
 0x4000 ----+--> translate ->| frame 2 |
                 (B's map)   +---------+
```

Same virtual address, different physical location, because each process has its own map.

## Before virtual memory

The earliest machines ran one program at a time, loaded at a fixed physical address. The program used physical addresses directly. That works until you want to run several programs at once (**multiprogramming**), and then three problems appear:

1. **Relocation.** Code containing fixed absolute addresses needs relocation or a translation mechanism when loaded elsewhere; position-independent code and relative addressing can reduce relocation work.
2. **Protection.** Nothing stops a buggy program writing over another program, or over the OS itself.
3. **Capacity.** Every program must fit in physical memory at once, and its size is limited by whatever contiguous space is free.

Virtual memory solves all three. In the framing of the OSTEP textbook, a good virtual memory system offers:

- **Transparency**: programs behave as if they have private memory and need no special code.
- **Efficiency**: translation must be fast (hardware does it) and the tables must not waste much space.
- **Protection and isolation**: a process cannot read or write memory outside its own address space, and it cannot touch the kernel's memory from user mode.

It also enables things the early designers did not have: sharing read-only library pages between processes, lazily allocating memory only when it is touched, and running programs whose memory is larger than RAM by spilling some to disk.

## Seeing it in C

This program forks a child. The child changes a global; the parent then prints the same variable.

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>

int x = 1;

int main(void) {
    pid_t pid = fork();
    if (pid < 0) {
        perror("fork");
        return 1;
    }
    if (pid == 0) {             /* child */
        x = 2;
        printf("child  %p %d\n",
               (void *)&x, x);
        return 0;
    }
    wait(NULL);                 /* parent */
    printf("parent %p %d\n", (void *)&x, x);
    return 0;
}
```

Illustrative output (the address varies):

```
child  0x55e4c3a1b010 2
parent 0x55e4c3a1b010 1
```

The child is a copy of the parent, so `x` sits at the same *virtual* address in both. But they have separate address spaces, so the child's write lands in a different physical frame and the parent still sees 1. (Lesson 4 explains how Linux makes this copy cheaply with copy-on-write.)

## What an address space looks like

A typical Linux x86-64 process maps selected regions of a much larger address range. This schematic assumes four-level paging; real layouts and mappings vary:

```
 0x7fff_ffff_ffff  lower canonical limit
 +-----------------+
 | stack           |  grows down
 |      ...        |
 | mmap region     |  libraries, mmap()
 |      ...        |
 | heap            |  grows up (brk)
 | .bss / .data    |  globals
 | .text           |  code, read-only
 +-----------------+
 0x0000_0000_0000  (normally unmapped)
```

You can see the real map of any process in `/proc/<pid>/maps`. Each line shows a range, its permissions (`r-xp` for code, `rw-p` for data) and what backs it (a file or nothing).

Points worth knowing:

- **Page 0 is normally left unmapped** to catch null-address accesses. Minimum-mapping policy and privileges can allow exceptions; a C null-pointer dereference is undefined behavior, not a portable promise of SIGSEGV.
- **ASLR** randomizes selected mappings when enabled; relocating executable code requires a suitable PIE executable. It makes address prediction harder, not impossible. `fork` preserves the parent's layout, including any randomized addresses.
- On x86-64, addresses are **canonical**: with 4-level paging, bits 63 to 47 must all be equal. Linux gives the lower half (0 to `0x00007fffffffffff`) to user space and keeps the upper half for the kernel.
- **Traditionally, kernel mappings appear in each process's page tables**, but its pages are marked supervisor-only, so user code gets a fault if it touches them. (After the 2018 Meltdown attack showed CPUs could leak that data speculatively, Linux added *kernel page-table isolation*, which unmaps most of the kernel while user code runs.)

## Base and bounds

The simplest hardware translation, used on machines in the 1960s, is **base and bounds** (also called dynamic relocation). The CPU has two registers per running process:

- **base**: where the process's memory starts in physical RAM;
- **bounds** (or limit): how big it is.

On every access the hardware does:

```
if virtual >= bounds:
    raise fault        # protection
physical = virtual + base
```

> [!example] Base and bounds
> A process is loaded at physical 32 KiB (base = 32,768) with bounds = 16 KiB (16,384).
> - Virtual 3,000 is below 16,384, so physical = 3,000 + 32,768 = **35,768**.
> - Virtual 20,000 is at or above 16,384, so the hardware raises a fault; an unhandled illegal access normally terminates the process.

On a context switch, the OS saves one process's base and bounds and loads the next. Only the kernel may change these registers; otherwise a process could simply point its base at someone else's memory.

Base and bounds gives relocation and protection cheaply, but it has two serious flaws:

- **Wasted space inside the process.** The whole address space must be contiguous in RAM, including the unused gap between heap and stack. A process with a large virtual range but little actual data still reserves the lot.
- **External fragmentation.** As processes of different sizes come and go, free RAM ends up as scattered holes. You may have 100 MiB free in total but no single hole big enough for a 20 MiB process.

## Segmentation

**Segmentation** generalises base and bounds: instead of one pair per process, there is one pair per logical **segment** (code, heap, stack and so on). Each segment can be placed anywhere in RAM independently, and the gap between heap and stack costs nothing.

The hardware needs to know which segment an address belongs to. One classic approach uses the top bits of the virtual address as a segment number.

> [!example] Segment translation
> A toy machine has 14-bit virtual addresses. The top 2 bits pick the segment and the low 12 bits are the offset.
>
> | Seg | Name | Base | Size |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | 00 | code | 0x8000 | 2 KiB |
> | 01 | heap | 0xA000 | 3 KiB |
>
> Virtual 0x1068 is `01 0000 0110 1000` in binary. Segment 01 (heap), offset 0x068 (104). 104 is less than 3 KiB, so physical = 0xA000 + 0x068 = **0xA068**.
>
> Virtual 0x0C10 is segment 00 (code), offset 0xC10 (3,088). That exceeds the 2 KiB (2,048) code segment, so the access faults. This is where the term **segmentation fault** comes from; Linux uses SIGSEGV for invalid accesses; native x86-64 Linux primarily enforces process memory isolation through paging rather than segment bounds.

Segments also carry **protection bits**. Code can be marked read-and-execute only, which makes it safe to **share** one copy of a program's code between many processes.

But segments are still variable-sized and contiguous, so segmentation still suffers **external fragmentation**. The OS has to search for holes (best fit, first fit) or periodically **compact** memory by copying segments together, which is slow. A heap segment that needs to grow may also find no free space next to it.

### The x86 story

Intel's processors carry the history with them:

- The **8086** (1978) formed a 20-bit physical address as `segment * 16 + offset`, mainly to reach 1 MiB with 16-bit registers.
- The **80286** added protected mode with segment descriptors holding base, limit and privilege level.
- The **80386** added **paging** underneath segmentation, and later 32-bit Linux systems used largely flat ordinary code/data segments with paging for isolation. Special segments and early Linux designs were exceptions.
- In **native x86-64 64-bit mode** (not its 32-bit compatibility submode), the hardware ignores the base and limit of the CS, DS, ES and SS segments. Only FS and GS bases survive, and they are used for thread-local storage (glibc points FS at each thread's TLS block).

For ordinary fixed-size page mappings, any suitable free frame can back a page. Physical fragmentation still matters for larger contiguous allocations, huge pages and device constraints. That is the subject of the next lesson.

## Where caches fit

CPU cache organization varies. A common design uses physical tags and a virtually indexed L1, allowing translation and cache-index lookup to overlap, but caches are a separate topic covered in the Computer Architecture subject. Here we care about the mapping, not about how fast RAM itself is.

## Pitfalls and misconceptions

- **"A pointer is a RAM address."** Not in user space. A pointer is meaningful only inside its own address space; passing its numeric value does not establish access in another process. Shared layouts can make pointers meaningful across processes; offsets within shared mappings are often more robust.
- **"Virtual memory means swap."** Swap is one feature built on virtual memory. Virtual memory is the translation layer, and it is in use on every access even on a phone with no swap at all.
- **"A big address space costs RAM."** The address space is mostly empty. Mappings can consume metadata and commit-accounting budget before resident pages are touched; resident backing, page tables and shared-page accounting also matter.

## Key takeaways
- Programs use virtual addresses; the MMU translates each one to a physical address using per-process tables set up by the OS.
- Virtual memory solves relocation, protection and capacity, and enables sharing and lazy allocation.
- Each Linux process has a mostly empty address space with code, data, heap, mmap and stack regions, randomised by ASLR; the kernel half is supervisor-only.
- Base and bounds adds a base and checks a limit: cheap, but wastes the gap inside the process and fragments RAM.
- Segmentation gives each logical region its own base and bounds; it still fragments externally, and x86-64 has all but abandoned it in favour of paging.

questions.prompt: A process runs under base-and-bounds translation with **base = 40,000** and **bounds = 8,000**. The program loads from virtual address **5,000**. Which physical address is accessed?

options.explanation: That is the virtual address. Under base and bounds the hardware always adds the base, so the program never sees its physical location.
Correct. 5,000 is less than the bounds of 8,000, so the access is legal, and physical = 5,000 + 40,000 = 45,000.
This adds the bounds to the base. The bounds is only used for the limit check, not in the address calculation.

options.text: It faults, because 5,000 is less than the base
options.explanation: The check compares the *virtual* address with the bounds, not with the base. Virtual addresses start at 0 for every process.

questions.workedExample:
Base and bounds does two things on every access:

1. **Check**: is virtual < bounds? 5,000 < 8,000, so yes, the access is allowed.
2. **Relocate**: physical = virtual + base = 5,000 + 40,000 = **45,000**.

The process's legal physical range is therefore 40,000 to 47,999. It can never reach anything outside that range, which is how the scheme provides protection.

options.text: Two different addresses; the child prints 2 and the parent prints 2
options.explanation: The child's write cannot reach the parent's memory, and the addresses will match because the child's address space is a copy of the parent's.

options.text: The same address twice; the child prints 2 and the parent prints 2
options.explanation: This assumes that the same virtual address means the same physical memory. Each process has its own mapping, so the child's write is invisible to the parent.

options.text: The same address twice; the child prints 2 and the parent prints 1
options.explanation: Correct. The child's address space is a copy of the parent's, so `&x` is the same virtual address, but it maps to a separate physical frame once the child writes.

options.text: Two different addresses; the child prints 2 and the parent prints 1
options.explanation: The values are right, but the addresses are the same: fork copies the address space layout exactly, including ASLR offsets.

questions.workedExample:
1. `fork()` creates a child whose address space is a duplicate of the parent's: the same regions at the same virtual addresses.
2. So `&x` is identical in both, for example `0x55e4c3a1b010`.
3. The child writes `x = 2`. That write goes through the *child's* page tables to the child's copy of the page.
4. The parent waits, then reads `x` through its own page tables and gets its own copy, still 1.

```
c 0x55e4c3a1b010 2
p 0x55e4c3a1b010 1
```

The lesson: a virtual address is only meaningful inside one address space.

questions.prompt: Which problems does virtual memory solve for a multiprogrammed OS? Select all that apply.

options.text: Relocation: a program can run wherever it is placed in RAM without rewriting its pointers
options.explanation: Correct. Each process uses its own virtual addresses, and the MMU maps them to wherever the OS put the data.

options.text: Protection: ordinary accesses cannot reach another process's private memory without an authorized mapping or access mechanism
options.explanation: Correct. A process can only reach physical memory that its own tables map, and kernel pages are supervisor-only.

options.text: Speed: memory accesses become faster than with physical addressing
options.explanation: Wrong. Translation adds work to every access; the TLB exists to make that overhead small, not negative.

options.text: Sharing: one copy of a library's code can be mapped into many processes
options.explanation: Correct. Several address spaces can map the same physical frames, typically read-only for code.

options.text: It removes the need for CPU caches
options.explanation: Wrong. Caches address the speed gap between the core and DRAM, an entirely separate problem from translation.

questions.workedExample: Virtual memory supports relocation, isolation and deliberate sharing through per-address-space mappings and permissions. Programs need not start at address zero. Translation has implementation cost; it is not a general promise of faster access. Caches remain useful and their indexing/tagging design interacts with translation. Shared code pages may be reused while process-private data remains separate.

questions.prompt: A process has **base = 100,000** and **bounds = 8,000**. It accesses virtual address **8,000**. What happens?

options.text: Physical address 108,000 is accessed
options.explanation: This is an off-by-one error. Legal virtual addresses are 0 to bounds − 1, so 8,000 is one past the end.

options.text: Physical address 8,000 is accessed
options.explanation: Base and bounds always adds the base; physical address 8,000 might belong to the kernel or another process.

options.text: The hardware raises a fault and the OS typically kills the process
options.explanation: Correct. The check is virtual < bounds. 8,000 is not less than 8,000, so the access is out of range.

options.text: The OS automatically grows the bounds to 8,001
options.explanation: The hardware faults; it does not automatically extend the region. The OS could grow in place if sufficient adjacent physical space were available, otherwise relocation or failure may be needed.

questions.workedExample:
1. Bounds is the **size** of the address space: 8,000 bytes means virtual addresses 0 to 7,999.
2. The hardware check is `virtual < bounds`.
3. 8,000 < 8,000 is false, so the MMU raises an exception before any memory is touched.
4. The OS's handler sees an illegal access by a user process and terminates it (the ancestor of today's SIGSEGV).

Off-by-one at the boundary is a classic exam trap, so always check whether the limit is a size or a last valid address. On real hardware it varies; in this model it is the size.

questions.prompt:
A toy machine uses 14-bit virtual addresses. The top 2 bits select the segment; the low 12 bits are the offset.

| Seg | Base | Size |
|---|---|---|
| 00 code | 0x4000 | 0x800 |
| 01 heap | 0x9000 | 0xC00 |

What does virtual address **0x1A40** translate to?

options.explanation: Correct. 0x1A40 is `01 1010 0100 0000`: segment 01 (heap), offset 0xA40. 0xA40 < 0xC00, so physical = 0x9000 + 0xA40 = 0x9A40.

options.text: 0xAA40
options.explanation: This adds the whole virtual address (0x1A40) to the base. The segment bits must be stripped off first; only the 12-bit offset is added.
This uses the code segment's base. The top two bits are 01, which selects the heap.

options.text: Segmentation fault, offset out of range
options.explanation: The offset 0xA40 (2,624) is below the heap size 0xC00 (3,072), so the access is legal.

questions.workedExample:
1. Write 0x1A40 in binary: `0001 1010 0100 0000`.
2. Keep the low 14 bits: `01 1010 0100 0000`.
3. Top two bits `01` select the **heap**.
4. Low 12 bits `1010 0100 0000` = **0xA40** = 2,624.
5. Bounds check: 0xA40 < 0xC00 (3,072). Legal.
6. Physical = base + offset = 0x9000 + 0xA40 = **0x9A40**.

Notice the hex trick: with a 12-bit offset, the last three hex digits *are* the offset, and the leading digit 1 here means segment 01.

questions.prompt: A segmentation-based system has 512 MiB of RAM. After hours of running, free memory consists of holes of 30 MiB, 25 MiB and 40 MiB (95 MiB in total). A new process needs a single 60 MiB segment. What is the problem, and what would solve it?

options.text: Internal fragmentation; use smaller segments
options.explanation: Internal fragmentation is wasted space *inside* an allocated block. Here the waste is between allocations, which is external fragmentation.

options.text: Thrashing; add swap space
options.explanation: Thrashing is about constant paging when the working set doesn't fit. This is a placement problem: the total is enough, but not contiguous.

options.text: External fragmentation; compact memory by moving segments together, or switch to fixed-size paging
options.explanation: Correct. 95 MiB is free, but no hole is 60 MiB. Compaction can merge the holes (slowly, by copying), and paging avoids the problem since any free frame can hold any page.

options.text: The process is simply too big; there is not enough free memory
options.explanation: There *is* enough in total (95 MiB > 60 MiB). The issue is that it is split into pieces too small to hold a contiguous segment.

questions.workedExample:
1. Total free: 30 + 25 + 40 = 95 MiB, which exceeds the 60 MiB needed.
2. A segment must be contiguous in physical memory. The largest hole is 40 MiB, so the request fails.
3. Free space split into unusable pieces *between* allocations is **external fragmentation**.
4. Fixes:
   - **Compaction**: stop processes, copy their segments together, update base registers. This leaves one 95 MiB hole but costs a lot of copying.
   - **Paging**: split memory into fixed-size frames. A 60 MiB region becomes 15,360 pages of 4 KiB that can go in any free frames.

questions.prompt: Why do ordinary Linux processes normally leave virtual page 0 unmapped (for example, addresses 0–4095 with 4 KiB pages)?

options.text: Because the BIOS interrupt table lives at physical address 0
options.explanation: That was true on real-mode PCs for *physical* address 0. Virtual page 0 could map to any frame; Linux leaves it unmapped for a different reason.

options.text: So that dereferencing a NULL pointer (or a small offset from it) faults immediately instead of reading or corrupting memory
options.explanation: Correct. A NULL dereference becomes a clean SIGSEGV, and there is also a `vm.mmap_min_addr` setting that stops processes mapping low pages, which blocks a class of kernel exploits.

options.text: Because the kernel's code is mapped there
options.explanation: On x86-64 Linux the kernel lives in the upper (negative) half of the address space, not at 0.

options.text: To save RAM, since page 0 would be wasted
options.explanation: An unmapped page costs no RAM whether it is at 0 or anywhere else; the choice of page 0 is about catching bugs.

questions.workedExample: On the stated Linux ABI a null pointer uses address zero. If generated code accesses that unmapped address, hardware faults and Linux normally delivers SIGSEGV. The C language itself makes null-pointer dereference undefined behavior. vm.mmap_min_addr restricts low mappings subject to configuration, capabilities and security policy; privileged exceptions exist. Low-mapping restrictions also mitigate some kernel null-dereference exploits.

questions.prompt: Which statements about segmentation on **x86-64 in 64-bit long mode** are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The base addresses of CS, DS, ES and SS are treated as 0
options.explanation: Correct. Long mode ignores these bases, giving a flat address space.

options.text: The FS and GS segment bases are still honoured, and are used for thread-local storage
options.explanation: Correct. glibc points FS at each thread's TLS block, and the kernel uses GS for per-CPU data.

options.text: Segment limits are checked on every data access, so Linux uses them to isolate processes
options.explanation: Wrong. Long mode does not check limits for these segments, and Linux isolates processes with page tables, not segments.

options.text: Paging is optional in long mode; segmentation can be used instead
options.explanation: Wrong. Long mode *requires* paging to be enabled. Segmentation is vestigial.

questions.workedExample: 8086 real mode computed segment×16+offset with 20-bit addressing. The 286 added protected segmentation; the 386 added paging. Later 32-bit Linux largely used flat code/data segments, with exceptions. Native 64-bit mode ignores CS/DS/ES/SS bases and ordinary segment limits, while FS/GS bases remain useful for TLS and per-CPU data. Compatibility mode has different segmentation semantics.

questions.prompt: On x86-64 with 4-level paging (48-bit virtual addresses), with address-tag masking disabled, which of these ordinary linear addresses is **non-canonical**, so that using it raises a fault even before any page table is consulted?

options.text: `0x00007fffffffffff`
options.explanation: Canonical. Bits 63 to 47 are all 0. This is the highest user-space address on Linux.
Canonical. Bits 63 to 47 are all 1. This is the bottom of the kernel half.
Correct. Bit 47 is 1 but bits 63 to 48 are 0. They must all equal bit 47, so this address lies in the non-canonical 'hole'.

options.text: `0xffffffffffffffff`
options.explanation: Canonical. Every bit is 1, so bits 63 to 47 agree; this is the last byte of the kernel half.

questions.workedExample:
1. With 48-bit addressing, only 48 bits are translated. The rule is that bits 63 to 48 must be **copies of bit 47** (sign-extension).
2. That splits the space into two halves:

```
0x0000_0000_0000_0000
  .. 0x0000_7fff_ffff_ffff  user
(hole: non-canonical)
0xffff_8000_0000_0000
  .. 0xffff_ffff_ffff_ffff  kernel
```

3. `0x0000800000000000` has bit 47 = 1 and bits 63 to 48 = 0, which is inconsistent, so it is in the hole.
4. An ordinary non-stack memory access to this non-canonical address raises a general-protection fault; stack references can instead raise a stack-segment fault. The hole exists so that future CPUs can translate more bits (5-level paging uses 57) without old software abusing the spare bits.

questions.prompt: 200 processes run the same program, whose code is 10 MiB. Under **base and bounds**, each process's code must sit inside its own contiguous region. Under **segmentation** with a shared, read-only code segment, all 200 can map the same physical copy. Roughly how much RAM does the code use in each case?

options.text: 10 MiB with base and bounds; 2,000 MiB with segmentation
options.explanation: This has the cases reversed. Sharing is what segmentation adds; base and bounds forces one copy per process.

options.text: 2,000 MiB in both, because each process needs its own copy
options.explanation: Read-only code never changes, so there is no reason for separate copies once the hardware can map one segment into many address spaces.

options.text: About 2,000 MiB with base and bounds; about 10 MiB with segmentation
options.explanation: Correct. 200 × 10 MiB = 2,000 MiB when each process needs its own copy, versus a single 10 MiB copy plus small per-process segment-table entries.

options.text: 10 MiB in both, because the OS deduplicates pages automatically
options.explanation: Base and bounds has no way to point part of one address space at another region; its single base register covers the whole process.

questions.workedExample:
1. **Base and bounds**: one base register per process covers its *entire* address space, code included. So each process holds its own 10 MiB copy: 200 × 10 = **2,000 MiB**.
2. **Segmentation**: each segment has its own base. Every process's code-segment entry can point at the *same* physical base, with protection bits set to read and execute only so no process can modify it.
3. Cost: one 10 MiB copy plus a few bytes of segment-table entry per process, about **10 MiB**.
4. Paging does the same at page granularity, which is how Linux shares libc and executables today.

questions.prompt: Assume a conventional 64-bit Linux process and ordinary generated memory-access instructions. Process A allocates a struct with malloc, then writes the raw pointer value (8 bytes) into a pipe. Process B, an unrelated program, reads those 8 bytes, casts them to a pointer, and dereferences it. What is the most likely outcome?

options.text: B reads A's struct, because the pointer is a physical RAM address
options.explanation: User-space pointers are virtual. B's MMU translates them with B's page tables, which don't include A's heap.

options.text: B reads A's struct, because both processes share one heap
options.explanation: Each process has its own heap. Only explicitly shared mappings (for example `mmap` with `MAP_SHARED`, or System V shared memory) are visible to both.

options.text: The kernel translates the pointer for B automatically when it passes through the pipe
options.explanation: Pipes copy bytes; they do not interpret or translate them.

options.text: B either segfaults (the address is unmapped in B) or silently reads unrelated data of its own
options.explanation: Correct. The value is just a number in B's address space: either nothing is mapped there (SIGSEGV) or something of B's is, and B reads that instead.

questions.workedExample: A raw pointer value names an address in A's mapping. Sending bytes through a pipe does not grant B access or relocate the pointer. B may fault on an unmapped/protected address or access unrelated mapped storage; portable C provides no defined cross-process dereference guarantee. To share data, establish a shared mapping and communicate offsets or identifiers with a defined representation and synchronization protocol.

questions.prompt: On x86-64 Linux, why did traditional process page tables include supervisor-only kernel mappings, and what does enabled kernel page-table isolation (KPTI) change?

options.text: So user code can call kernel functions directly; KPTI made these calls go through the syscall instruction
options.explanation: User code could never call kernel functions directly: kernel pages are supervisor-only and fault from user mode.

options.text: So system calls and interrupts can run kernel code without switching page tables; KPTI unmaps most of the kernel while in user mode, at the cost of a page-table switch on every kernel entry and exit
options.explanation: Correct. Keeping the kernel mapped avoids a CR3 switch per syscall. Meltdown let user code speculatively read supervisor-only pages, so KPTI uses separate user tables with only a small trampoline mapped.

options.text: To save RAM by sharing kernel memory; KPTI duplicated the kernel per process
options.explanation: KPTI maintains separate user/kernel page-table views with some shared structures and additional tables. It does not duplicate the kernel's code/data per process.

options.text: Because 64-bit CPUs require it; KPTI moved the kernel to the lower half
options.explanation: No architecture requirement forces this layout, and KPTI didn't move the kernel; it changed what is mapped while user code runs.

questions.workedExample:
1. Before KPTI: each process's page tables include the kernel's mappings, marked supervisor-only (the U/S bit clear). A syscall changes the privilege level but **not** CR3, so no page-table switch and no TLB flush.
2. Protection relied on the permission check: user-mode access to those pages faults.
3. **Meltdown** (2018) showed that on many Intel CPUs the data could be loaded speculatively *before* the fault, then leaked through cache timing.
4. **KPTI**: while in user mode, the active page tables map only kernel mappings needed for entry/exit and related CPU structures. On entry from user mode, the kernel switches CR3 to the full tables, and back on return.
5. Cost: extra CR3 writes and potential TLB misses on every kernel crossing. PCIDs (lesson 3) reduce the cost by letting both sets of translations stay in the TLB.

lessons.title: Paging and page tables
lessons.summary: Pages and frames, what a page table entry holds, translating an address bit by bit, and why x86-64 uses a 4- or 5-level tree of tables.
lessons.body:
Segmentation chopped memory into variable-sized pieces and paid for it with external fragmentation. **Paging** takes the opposite approach: chop *everything* into small, fixed-size blocks.

- The virtual address space is divided into **pages**.
- Physical memory is divided into **frames** (or page frames) of the same size.
- A **page table** records, for each virtual page, which physical frame holds it.

For a fixed base-page size, any suitable free frame can back a page; an ordinary virtual region need not occupy one physical hole. Physical contiguity still matters for huge pages and some device/kernel allocations. A process's pages can be scattered all over RAM while appearing perfectly contiguous to the program.

On x86-64 the standard page size is **4 KiB** (4,096 bytes), with optional huge pages of 2 MiB and 1 GiB.

## Splitting an address

Since a page is 4,096 = 2^12 bytes, the low 12 bits of an address say where you are *inside* the page. The remaining high bits say *which* page.

```
 virtual address
 +------------------+------------+
 | virtual page no. |  offset    |
 |      (VPN)       |  12 bits   |
 +------------------+------------+
          | page table lookup
          v
 +------------------+------------+
 |  frame no. (PFN) |  offset    |
 +------------------+------------+
 physical address
```

Translation replaces the VPN with the PFN and keeps the offset unchanged. The offset never needs translating because a page and its frame have the same internal layout.

> [!example] A toy translation
> A machine has 16-bit addresses and 4 KiB pages: 4 bits of VPN, 12 bits of offset, so 16 virtual pages. The page table says VPN 3 maps to PFN 7.
>
> Virtual 0x3A7C: VPN = 0x3, offset = 0xA7C. Replace 3 with 7: physical **0x7A7C**.
>
> With 4 KiB pages, the last three hex digits are always the offset, which makes hex translation quick by eye.

Here is the same idea in Python:

```python
PAGE_BITS = 12
OFF_MASK = (1 << PAGE_BITS) - 1
page_table = {0: 5, 1: 9, 3: 7}  # VPN->PFN

def translate(va):
    vpn = va >> PAGE_BITS
    off = va & OFF_MASK
    if vpn not in page_table:
        raise MemoryError("page fault")
    pfn = page_table[vpn]
    return (pfn << PAGE_BITS) | off

print(hex(translate(0x3A7C)))  # 0x7a7c
print(hex(translate(0x0123)))  # 0x5123
translate(0x2000)  # VPN 2: page fault
```

## What a page table entry holds

A **page table entry (PTE)** is more than a frame number. For ordinary x86-64 4 KiB leaf mappings, entries are 8 bytes. The table summarizes selected fields; implemented physical-address width and enabled CPU features constrain their interpretation:

| Bit(s) | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | P | Present: mapping valid |
| 1 | R/W | Writable |
| 2 | U/S | User mode may access |
| 5 | A | Accessed (set by CPU) |
| 6 | D | Dirty: page written |
| 8 | G | Global translation when enabled |
| 12–51 | PFN field | Address bits, limited by MAXPHYADDR |
| 63 | NX | No-execute |

The OS sets P, R/W, U/S and NX to express permissions. The CPU maintains **A** and **D** for translation use and writes. After clearing them, the OS must use the required invalidation protocol to observe later accesses reliably; cached translations do not promise a fresh in-memory bit update on every access. The OS reads those bits later to decide what to evict (lesson 5) and whether an evicted page must be written to disk first.

If P is 0, the hardware ignores the rest of the entry and raises a **page fault**. The OS can encode software state such as swap information in a non-present entry, while respecting architectural and security constraints. Non-present entries must not be treated as unconstrained storage on every implementation.

For ordinary user-mode accesses with NX support enabled and coherent translations, writing through R/W=0, reading a supervisor-only mapping, or executing an NX mapping faults. Supervisor write protection depends on control state; cached translations must be invalidated after changing permissions. This is how code is made read-only and data non-executable.

## The size problem

A single flat array with one PTE per virtual page is simple, but consider its size.

- **32-bit**, 4 KiB pages, 4-byte entries: 2^32 / 2^12 = 2^20 entries × 4 B = **4 MiB per process**. Tolerable, but it adds up across hundreds of processes.
- **48-bit** (x86-64), 4 KiB pages, 8-byte entries: 2^36 entries × 8 B = 2^39 B = **512 GiB** for the full 48-bit space. This is an impractical flat-table overhead for ordinary processes.

Yet a typical process uses only a few hundred MiB scattered across a 128 TiB space. Nearly all of the flat table would say "not present". The fix is to avoid storing those empty stretches.

## Multi-level page tables

The trick is to **page the page table**. Split the VPN into several chunks and build a tree. The top-level table points to second-level tables, and so on. If an entire region is unused, the upper entry is simply marked not-present, and the tables below it are never allocated.

x86-64 uses a 4-level tree for 48-bit addresses. Each table is exactly one 4 KiB page holding 512 entries of 8 bytes, so each level consumes 9 bits of the address (2^9 = 512):

```
47   39 38   30 29   21 20   12 11     0
+------+------+------+------+--------+
| PML4 | PDPT |  PD  |  PT  | offset |
|  9   |  9   |  9   |  9   |   12   |
+------+------+------+------+--------+
```

9 + 9 + 9 + 9 + 12 = 48 bits. Bits 63 to 48 must be copies of bit 47 (the canonical-address rule).

| Intel name | Linux name | One entry covers |
|---|---|---|
| PML4 | PGD (P4D folded) | 512 GiB |
| PDPT | PUD | 1 GiB |
| PD | PMD | 2 MiB |
| PT | PTE | 4 KiB |

The physical address of the top-level table lives in the **CR3** register. A context switch to another process loads its CR3 value, and that one register write switches the whole address space.

### A walk, bit by bit

Translate the virtual address **0x7ffd4a3b2c18** (a typical stack address). First write the 48 bits in binary and cut them into fields:

```
0x7ffd4a3b2c18 =
011111111 111110101 001010001
110110010 110000011000

PML4 = 011111111   = 255
PDPT = 111110101   = 501
PD   = 001010001   = 81
PT   = 110110010   = 434
off  = 110000011000 = 0xc18
```

The same split in code:

```python
def split(va):
    off  =  va        & 0xFFF
    pt   = (va >> 12) & 0x1FF
    pd   = (va >> 21) & 0x1FF
    pdpt = (va >> 30) & 0x1FF
    pml4 = (va >> 39) & 0x1FF
    return pml4, pdpt, pd, pt, off

print(split(0x7ffd4a3b2c18))
# (255, 501, 81, 434, 3096)
```

(3,096 is 0xc18.) Now the MMU walks the tree:

```
CR3 -> PML4 table
       entry 255 -> PDPT table
         entry 501 -> PD table
           entry 81 -> PT table
             entry 434 -> PFN 0x1a2b3
physical = (0x1a2b3 << 12) | 0xc18
         = 0x1a2b3c18
```

At each level the hardware reads one 8-byte entry, checks the present and permission bits, and takes the next table's physical address from bits 12 to 51. If any level's entry is not present, the walk stops with a page fault.

> [!warning] Four extra memory reads
> A naive walk costs **four memory accesses** before the real one, a 5× slowdown if every access had to do it. The TLB (next lesson) caches finished translations so that most accesses skip the walk entirely.

### How much space does it save?

Imagine a small process whose code and heap sit in one 2 MiB region near the bottom of the address space and whose stack sits near the top.

- 1 PML4 table (always needed).
- Code and heap: 1 PDPT, 1 PD, 1 PT.
- Stack: a different PML4 entry, so its own PDPT, PD and PT.

That is 7 tables × 4 KiB = **28 KiB** of page tables, against 512 GiB for a flat table. Ignoring kernel mappings, KPTI and other process regions, this toy count assumes the stack also fits within one 2 MiB region. Table cost depends on mapped address distribution as well as size: each fully used PT maps 2 MiB for 4 KiB of table, about 0.2% overhead.

## Huge pages fall out naturally

A PD entry normally points to a PT. If its **PS** (page size) bit is set, it instead points directly to a 2 MiB-aligned 2 MiB frame, and the walk stops one level early. The low **21 bits** of the address become the offset.

Likewise a PDPT entry with PS set maps a **1 GiB** page with a 30-bit offset. Lesson 3 explains why huge pages matter for TLB performance.

## Five-level paging

48 bits gives 256 TiB of virtual space, and the architecture allows up to 52-bit physical addresses (4 PiB). Some very large servers wanted more virtual space, so Intel added **5-level paging** (LA57), available on supporting CPU models.

In five-level mode, PML5 is Linux PGD and PML4 is Linux P4D. In four-level mode P4D is folded and PML4 acts as PGD. 9 × 5 + 12 = **57 bits**, or 128 PiB of virtual space.

Linux supports it when built with the option and run on a capable CPU. To avoid breaking programs that stash tags in the high bits of pointers, Linux hands out addresses above the 47-bit boundary only if a program asks for one explicitly by passing a high hint address to `mmap`.

Five-level paging can add a lookup to an uncached walk. A capable kernel can enable it on supported hardware even for small-memory workloads; unsupported hardware uses the folded four-level configuration.

## Other designs

Not every architecture uses a radix tree:

- **Inverted page tables** keep entries indexed by physical frame, with a lookup mechanism such as a hash index over address-space identity and virtual page number. They are distinct from a hashed forward mapping table; not every architecture using hashed translation has one entry per physical frame.
- ARM64 uses a tree very like x86-64's, with a choice of 4 KiB, 16 KiB or 64 KiB granules. Apple's M-series Macs use 16 KiB pages.

## Trade-offs and pitfalls

- **Internal fragmentation.** Memory is handed out in whole pages. An independently backed 1-byte region can occupy a whole base page once allocated. Average half-page waste assumes roughly uniform allocation remainders; sharing, lazy allocation and suballocation change the result. Bigger pages can increase waste.
- **Page tables cost real memory.** A dense, populated 100 GiB mapping with 4 KiB pages needs about 200 MiB of leaf page tables (100 GiB / 2 MiB per PT × 4 KiB). Many processes sharing a large mapping each pay that separately, which is one reason big databases use huge pages.
- **Don't confuse page-aligned with frame-contiguous.** Two adjacent virtual pages can be in frames gigabytes apart. DMA mappings must meet the device's requirements; options include scatter/gather lists, IOMMU translation or physically contiguous buffers.

## Key takeaways
- Paging removes the requirement that an ordinary virtual region fit one physical hole; huge and contiguous allocations can still suffer fragmentation.
- An address splits into a page number and an offset; translation swaps the page number for a frame number and keeps the offset.
- PTEs carry permission bits (present, writable, user, no-execute) and hardware-maintained accessed and dirty bits.
- A flat page table for 48-bit addresses would be 512 GiB; x86-64 uses a 4-level tree of 512-entry tables indexed by 9 bits each, rooted at CR3.
- A PS bit at the PD or PDPT level makes a 2 MiB or 1 GiB huge page; 5-level paging extends addresses to 57 bits.
- A full walk costs four memory reads, which is why the TLB exists.

## Further reading
- [OSTEP: Paging: Introduction (PDF)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-paging.pdf)
- [OSTEP: Paging: Smaller Tables (PDF)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-smalltables.pdf)
- [Page tables — Linux kernel documentation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/mm/page_tables.html)
- [x86_64 memory map — Linux kernel documentation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/arch/x86/x86_64/mm.html)
- [Five-level page tables — LWN.net](https://lwn.net/Articles/717293/)
- [Intel 5-level paging — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel_5-level_paging)
- [Page table — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Page_table)

questions.prompt: A system uses 4 KiB pages. The page table maps **VPN 0x5 to PFN 0x12**. What physical address does virtual address **0x5ABC** translate to?

options.text: 0x5ABC
options.explanation: This forgets to translate at all: the page number must be replaced by the frame number.

options.text: 0x12ABC
options.explanation: Correct. Offset = low 12 bits = 0xABC; VPN = 0x5 maps to PFN 0x12; physical = 0x12 followed by 0xABC.

options.text: 0x17ABC
options.explanation: This adds the PFN to the VPN (0x12 + 0x5 = 0x17). Paging *replaces* the page number; it does not add a base like base-and-bounds.

options.text: 0x120ABC
options.explanation: This shifts the PFN by 16 bits instead of 12. With 4 KiB pages the offset is 12 bits, i.e. exactly three hex digits.

questions.workedExample:
1. 4 KiB = 2^12, so the offset is the low **12 bits**: three hex digits.
2. 0x5ABC → VPN = 0x5, offset = 0xABC.
3. Look up VPN 0x5 → PFN 0x12.
4. Physical = (PFN << 12) | offset = 0x12000 | 0xABC = **0x12ABC**.

Shortcut: with 4 KiB pages, write the PFN and then append the last three hex digits of the virtual address.

questions.prompt: A system uses **16 KiB** pages and 48-bit virtual addresses. How many bits of each virtual address form the page offset, and how many form the virtual page number?

options.text: 12-bit offset, 36-bit VPN
options.explanation: Those are the numbers for 4 KiB pages. A 16 KiB page needs 2 more offset bits.

options.text: 16-bit offset, 32-bit VPN
options.explanation: 2^16 is 64 KiB, so this would be the split for 64 KiB pages.

options.text: 14-bit offset, 34-bit VPN
options.explanation: Correct. 16 KiB = 2^14 bytes, so 14 bits locate a byte within a page, leaving 48 − 14 = 34 bits of page number.

options.text: 14-bit offset, 48-bit VPN
options.explanation: The VPN is what is *left* after the offset: the two fields together make up the 48-bit address.

questions.workedExample:
1. Offset bits = log2(page size). 16 KiB = 16 × 1024 = 16,384 = **2^14**, so 14 bits.
2. VPN bits = address bits − offset bits = 48 − 14 = **34**.
3. Sanity check: 2^34 pages × 2^14 bytes per page = 2^48 bytes, the whole address space.

16 KiB is a supported ARM64 translation granule; this question explicitly assumes a 48-bit virtual address width.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit system uses 4 KiB pages and a **single-level (flat)** page table with 4-byte entries. How large is each process's page table?

options.text: 4 KiB
options.explanation: That is one page, enough for 1,024 entries, which maps only 4 MiB of address space.

options.text: 1 MiB
options.explanation: This counts the number of entries (2^20) but forgets each entry is 4 bytes.

options.text: 4 GiB
options.explanation: That is the size of the whole 32-bit address space, not of the table describing it.

options.text: 4 MiB
options.explanation: Correct. 2^32 / 2^12 = 2^20 pages, each needing a 4-byte entry: 2^22 bytes = 4 MiB, even if the process uses almost none of it.

questions.workedExample:
1. Number of virtual pages = 2^32 / 2^12 = 2^20 = 1,048,576.
2. A flat table needs one entry per page, used or not.
3. Size = 2^20 × 4 bytes = 2^22 bytes = **4 MiB** per process.
4. With 200 processes that is 800 MiB just for page tables, which is why even 32-bit x86 used a two-level table (a page directory of 1,024 entries pointing to page tables of 1,024 entries).

questions.prompt: On x86-64 with 4-level paging, which table indices does the MMU use to translate virtual address **0x0000004020123456**?

options.text: PML4 0, PDPT 256, PD 256, PT 291, offset 0x456
options.explanation: Correct. Shift and mask 9 bits at a time: bits 47–39 = 0, 38–30 = 256, 29–21 = 256, 20–12 = 291 (0x123), and the low 12 bits are 0x456.

options.text: PML4 0, PDPT 1, PD 1, PT 0x123, offset 0x456
options.explanation: This reads the hex digits as if each level were a 4-bit or 8-bit field. Each level is 9 bits, which does not line up with hex digits.

options.text: PML4 1, PDPT 0, PD 256, PT 291, offset 0x456
options.explanation: This assigns bit 38 to the PML4 field. The PML4 index is bits 47 to 39, all of which are 0 here.

options.text: PML4 0, PDPT 256, PD 256, PT 291, offset 0x3456
options.explanation: The offset is only 12 bits (three hex digits); the 0x3 belongs to the PT index.

questions.workedExample:
Do it with shifts:

```
va = 0x4020123456
off  = va & 0xFFF          = 0x456
pt   = (va >> 12) & 0x1FF  = 0x123
                           = 291
pd   = (va >> 21) & 0x1FF  = 256
pdpt = (va >> 30) & 0x1FF  = 256
pml4 = (va >> 39) & 0x1FF  = 0
```

Check one: `0x4020123456 >> 30` = 0x100 = 256, and 256 & 511 = 256.

Or think in binary: 0x40_2012_3456 has bit 38 set (giving PDPT 256, since 2^38 / 2^30 = 256) and bit 29 set (PD 2^29 / 2^21 = 256).

questions.prompt: A single load stays within a present 4 KiB page on x86-64 with four-level paging. It misses all translation and page-walk caches. Count one read per paging level plus the data read, ignoring accessed-bit updates, nested virtualization and data-cache effects. How many reads does this model require?

options.explanation: That would only be true on a TLB hit, when the translation is already cached.
Four accesses are needed for the walk, but the load itself still has to read the data afterwards.
Correct. One read from each of the PML4, PDPT, PD and PT tables, then the actual data access.
That is the cost with a single-level page table: one PTE read plus the data.

questions.workedExample: Read PML4, PDPT, PD and PT entries, then the requested data: five reads in this simplified model. It is not a prediction of 5× wall-clock latency: cache hits, overlapping work and other hardware behavior matter. A five-level full walk adds one entry read.

questions.prompt: For ordinary user-mode x86-64 accesses, with NX enabled and no stale cached translations, which conditions cause a page fault? Assume canonical addresses and all other permissions permit the access. Select all that apply.

options.text: Reading a page whose PTE has the Present bit clear
options.explanation: Correct. A non-present entry always faults; the kernel then decides whether to load the page or send SIGSEGV.

options.text: Writing to a page whose PTE has R/W clear
options.explanation: Correct. Write-protection violations fault. Copy-on-write relies on exactly this.

options.text: User-mode code reading a page whose PTE has U/S clear
options.explanation: Correct. Supervisor-only pages fault from user mode; this protects the kernel's mappings.

options.text: Reading a page whose Dirty bit is clear
options.explanation: Wrong. D = 0 just means the page hasn't been written since the bit was last cleared. The CPU sets it on the next write, with no fault.

options.text: Executing code from a page with the NX bit set
options.explanation: Correct. Instruction fetches from no-execute pages fault, which blocks code injected into data or the stack.

questions.workedExample: In this model, non-present mappings, writes forbidden by R/W, user accesses forbidden by U/S and execution forbidden by NX fault. Clear A/D bits are bookkeeping state rather than a reason to reject an otherwise permitted access. Hardware-maintained A/D state and permission changes still require correct OS invalidation protocols; this is not a full specification of every paging mode.

questions.prompt: A process using four-level x86-64 paging maps and touches exactly **1 GiB** of contiguous, 1 GiB-aligned virtual memory using 4 KiB pages. Approximately how much memory do its page tables need for that region?

options.text: About 4 KiB
options.explanation: That is a single PT, which maps only 2 MiB.

options.text: About 2 MiB
options.explanation: Correct. 1 GiB / 2 MiB = 512 PTs at 4 KiB each = 2 MiB, plus one PD, one PDPT and the PML4 (12 KiB): about 2 MiB.

options.text: About 512 MiB
options.explanation: This seems to compute one 4 KiB table per 8 KiB of memory. Each PT holds 512 entries and maps 2 MiB.

options.text: About 2 GiB
options.explanation: Page tables are about 0.2% of the memory mapped with 4 KiB pages, not twice as large.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each PTE maps 4 KiB. One PT has 512 entries, so it maps 512 × 4 KiB = **2 MiB**.
2. Number of PTs for 1 GiB: 1,024 MiB / 2 MiB = **512**.
3. PT memory: 512 × 4 KiB = **2 MiB**.
4. Upper levels: one PD (its 512 entries point to those 512 PTs), one PDPT entry, one PML4 entry. About 3 more pages = 12 KiB.
5. Total ≈ **2 MiB**, about 0.2% overhead.

With 2 MiB pages, the leaf PTs vanish and one 4 KiB PD covers the region, plus the required upper tables. With a 1 GiB page, one PDPT entry covers it, still within allocated upper tables. Existing tables may be reused.

questions.prompt: A process uses a **2 MiB huge page**. The PD entry for virtual address **0x7f0012345678** has PS = 1 and points to the 2 MiB frame starting at physical **0x40000000**. What is the physical address?

options.explanation: This uses a 12-bit offset as for a 4 KiB page. With a 2 MiB page the offset is 21 bits.
This keeps 24 bits (six hex digits) as the offset. 21 bits is 0x1FFFFF, so bit 21 (the 0x2 in 0x345678) belongs to the PD index.
The address still has to be translated; huge pages change the size of the page, not whether translation happens.
Correct. A 2 MiB page has a 21-bit offset: 0x7f0012345678 & 0x1FFFFF = 0x145678. Add it to the frame base: 0x40145678.

questions.workedExample:
1. 2 MiB = 2^21, so the offset is the low **21 bits**: mask with `0x1FFFFF`.
2. The low five hex digits, 0x45678, are bits 0 to 19. Bit 20 is the lowest bit of the next digit, 0x3 = `0011`. Keep that bit (1) and drop the rest (bit 21 belongs to the PD index), so the sixth digit becomes 0x1.

```
0x345678 & 0x1FFFFF = 0x145678
```

3. The walk stops at the PD (PS = 1), so there is no PT lookup.
4. Physical = 0x40000000 + 0x145678 = **0x40145678**.

questions.prompt: Suppose an architecture uses **64 KiB pages** and 8-byte page table entries, with each table occupying exactly one page. How many levels are needed to translate a **48-bit** virtual address?

options.explanation: Two levels of 13 bits plus a 16-bit offset covers only 42 bits, 6 short of 48.
Correct. Offset = 16 bits, each table has 65,536 / 8 = 8,192 = 2^13 entries, so each level covers 13 bits. 48 − 16 = 32 bits need ceil(32 / 13) = 3 levels.
Four levels is the x86-64 answer for 4 KiB pages (9 bits per level). Larger pages mean both a bigger offset and more bits per level.
Five levels is x86-64 with 57-bit addresses and 4 KiB pages.

questions.workedExample:
1. Offset bits = log2(64 KiB) = **16**.
2. Entries per table = page size / entry size = 65,536 / 8 = 8,192 = 2^13, so each level resolves **13 bits**.
3. Bits to translate = 48 − 16 = **32**.
4. Levels = ceil(32 / 13) = ceil(2.46) = **3**. The top level is only partly used (32 − 26 = 6 bits).

This matches ARM64 with the 64 KiB granule, which uses 3 levels for 48-bit addresses (and 2 levels for 42-bit). Bigger pages mean shallower trees and fewer memory accesses per TLB miss, at the cost of more internal fragmentation.

questions.prompt: Which statements about multi-level page tables are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: They save memory when the address space is sparse, because unused regions need no lower-level tables
options.explanation: Correct. A not-present upper entry stands in for a whole 512 GiB, 1 GiB or 2 MiB region.

options.text: An uncached multi-level walk to a base-page leaf requires more entry reads than a flat-table lookup
options.explanation: Correct. A flat table needs one PTE read; a 4-level tree needs four. That is the price of the space saving.

options.text: If every virtual page were mapped, the tree would use slightly more memory than a flat table
options.explanation: Correct. The leaf tables equal the flat table in total, and the upper levels add a little on top.

options.text: They eliminate internal fragmentation
options.explanation: Wrong. Internal fragmentation comes from rounding allocations up to whole pages, which is unaffected by how the page table is organised.

questions.workedExample: Sparse mappings can omit entire lower-level subtrees, with overhead depending on their address distribution. An uncached base-page walk reads one entry per level; paging-structure caches and huge leaves reduce that work. A fully populated tree uses the flat table's worth of leaf entries plus upper tables. Page-granularity allocation can still waste space; lazy allocation or suballocation changes actual resident usage.

questions.prompt: In a four-level x86-64 model, 50 PostgreSQL backends fully populate an aligned 64 GiB shared region. Assume each backend has independent page-table pages, no HugeTLB PMD sharing, and ignore upper-table overhead. How much leaf-table memory is needed with 4 KiB pages versus 2 MiB pages?

options.text: About 128 MiB with 4 KiB pages; about 256 KiB with huge pages
options.explanation: These are the figures for one process. Each process has its own page tables, even for a shared region, so multiply by 50.

options.text: About 6.25 GiB with 4 KiB pages; about 12.5 MiB with 2 MiB pages
options.explanation: Correct. 64 GiB / 2 MiB = 32,768 PTs × 4 KiB = 128 MiB per process, × 50 = 6,400 MiB. With 2 MiB pages, 64 PDs × 4 KiB = 256 KiB per process, × 50 = 12.5 MiB.

options.text: Nothing extra: shared memory shares its page tables too
options.explanation: The ordinary data pages are shared, while page-table sharing depends on mapping type and implementation. This question explicitly assumes independent tables; eligible Linux HugeTLB mappings may share PMD tables.

options.text: About 64 GiB, the same as the data
options.explanation: Page tables cost about 0.2% of mapped memory with 4 KiB pages, not 100%.

questions.workedExample: For 4 KiB mappings, each backend needs 64 GiB / 2 MiB = 32,768 leaf PTs. At 4 KiB each that is 128 MiB per backend; 50 × 128 MiB = 6,400 MiB = 6.25 GiB. For 2 MiB mappings, 64 PDs × 4 KiB = 256 KiB per backend; 50 copies total 12.5 MiB. These are leaf-table estimates under the stated no-sharing assumption. Linux HugeTLB may share PMD tables for eligible mappings, and actual memory also depends on population, alignment and upper levels. PostgreSQL documents reduced table overhead as a benefit of huge_pages.

questions.prompt: The scheduler switches between tasks with different userspace memory contexts on x86-64. Which hardware register selects the new address-space root?

options.text: Copies B's page tables into a fixed kernel location that the MMU always reads
options.explanation: There is no fixed location: the MMU reads whatever tree CR3 points to, so copying would be pointless and very slow.

options.text: Rewrites every PTE in the shared page table to point to B's frames
options.explanation: Each process has its own tree. Rewriting entries would cost time proportional to B's memory on every switch.

options.text: Swaps A's memory out to disk and B's back in
options.explanation: Both processes can be resident at once; paging to disk is unrelated to a context switch.

options.text: Loads the physical address of B's top-level table into CR3
options.explanation: Correct. One register write switches the whole address space. Without PCIDs this also flushes non-global TLB entries; lesson 3 covers how PCIDs avoid that.

lessons.title: The TLB and huge pages
lessons.summary: How the translation lookaside buffer makes paging fast, effective access time calculations, TLB reach, ASIDs and PCIDs across context switches, shootdowns, and when huge pages help or hurt.
lessons.body:
The previous lesson ended with a problem. An uncached four-level x86-64 walk to a 4 KiB page reads four entries before the data access. That simplified read count is not a universal 5× latency prediction.

Hardware fixes this with a small, very fast cache of recent translations: the **translation lookaside buffer (TLB)**. Most memory accesses find their translation in the TLB and skip the walk entirely.

## What the TLB stores

Each TLB entry maps one virtual page to one physical frame, with the permission bits copied from the PTE:

```
 TLB entry
 +---------+---------+---------------+
 |   VPN   |   PFN   | R/W U/S NX .. |
 +---------+---------+---------------+
   tag       data      permissions
```

On every memory access the MMU does:

1. Look up the VPN in the TLB.
2. **Hit**: take the PFN, check permissions, and form the physical address. Many designs overlap lookup with cache indexing; actual latency and throughput depend on the CPU.
3. **Miss**: walk the page tables (the hardware **page walker** on x86 and ARM), insert the result into the TLB, then retry.

Some older architectures, notably MIPS, use a **software-managed TLB**: a miss raises an exception and the OS refills the entry itself. That gives the OS freedom over page-table format with handler cost depending on the architecture and implementation. x86 and ARM do it in hardware.

## Typical sizes and costs

TLB organizations differ by CPU, page size and instruction/data access type. Many cores have separate first-level instruction/data TLBs and another translation-cache level. Consult the exact CPU's documentation or hardware enumeration rather than assuming one capacity.

A miss served by another translation cache avoids a full walk. Page walks can use data caches and paging-structure caches; a TLB miss is not synonymous with a DRAM access or an OS page fault.

> [!note] Content gap
> Universal entry counts and cycle/microsecond costs are omitted: this lesson has no measured CPU configuration or reproducible benchmark record for those figures. The following capacities and times are explicit arithmetic examples.

## Why hit rates are high

The TLB works for the same reason caches work: **locality**.

> [!example] Scanning an array
> A loop reads a large array of 4-byte ints in order. Each 4 KiB page holds 1,024 ints.
>
> In a cold, aligned scalar-access model without translation prefetching or interfering evictions, the first access to each page misses and the next 1,023 hit. That is 1 miss per 1,024 accesses: a **99.9%** hit rate.
>
> Now read only one int per page (stride 4,096 bytes). Every access lands on a new page. On a cold pass without translation prefetching, each newly visited page misses. On repeated passes, capacity and replacement determine the hit rate.

```c
/* Same address range, different
   access counts and TLB miss rates. */
for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++)
    sum += a[i];        /* stride 4 B */

for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i += 1024)
    sum += a[i];        /* stride 4 KiB */
```

On supported Linux PMUs, `perf stat -e dTLB-load-misses ./prog` can help investigate. Check `perf list`, event semantics, permissions and CPU model: a generic event need not count every L1-TLB miss.

Random access over a large data structure (a big hash table, a graph, a B-tree spread across GiB of RAM) is the hard case. Each access may touch a different page, and the TLB cannot hold them all.

## Effective access time

The **effective access time (EAT)** is the average cost of one memory access once TLB misses are included:

```
EAT = h * hit_cost + (1 - h) * miss_cost
```

where `h` is the TLB hit rate.

> [!example] Single-level table
> Memory access = 100 ns, TLB lookup time negligible, single-level page table, hit rate 98%.
> - Hit: 100 ns (just the data).
> - Miss: 100 ns for the PTE + 100 ns for the data = 200 ns.
> - EAT = 0.98 × 100 + 0.02 × 200 = 98 + 4 = **102 ns**, a 2% slowdown.

> [!example] x86-64, 4-level, no walk caching
> Same 100 ns memory, but a miss costs 4 table reads + the data = 500 ns.
> - At 99% hits: 0.99 × 100 + 0.01 × 500 = 99 + 5 = **104 ns**.
> - At 90% hits: 0.90 × 100 + 0.10 × 500 = 90 + 50 = **140 ns**, a 40% slowdown.

If the TLB lookup itself takes time `t` (older textbooks often use 20 ns), add `t` to both the hit and the miss cost. The lesson is the same: the hit rate dominates, and every percentage point of misses costs a multiple of itself once the walk is deep.

## TLB reach

**TLB reach** is the amount of memory the TLB can map at once: entries × page size.

| TLB | 4 KiB pages | 2 MiB pages |
|---|---|---|
| 64 entries | 256 KiB | 128 MiB |
| 1,536 entries | 6 MiB | 3 GiB |

A hot set beyond the effective reach can increase misses; locality, associativity, page-size-specific capacities and other translation-cache levels determine the rate. If all 50 GiB of a buffer pool is actively accessed, it greatly exceeds a hypothetical 6 MiB reach. Allocated pool capacity need not equal the hot working set. This is the main argument for huge pages.

## Context switches, ASIDs and PCIDs

A TLB entry says "VPN 0x400 maps to PFN 0x9a2". That is only true for one address space. When the kernel switches to another process (by loading CR3), the old entries become wrong.

The simple fix, and the traditional x86 behaviour, is to **flush the TLB** on every CR3 write. The new process then starts cold and pays a burst of misses.

Two features reduce the damage:

- **Global pages.** PTEs with the **G** bit set survive a CR3 write. Kernel mappings, identical in every process, were marked global so they stayed cached across switches.
- **Address-space identifiers.** Tags let translations from several address spaces coexist, reducing flushes. Mapping changes and tag reuse still require invalidation. ARM and MIPS call these **ASIDs**. On x86 they are **PCIDs** (process-context identifiers): 12 bits held in the low bits of CR3, so up to 4,096 tags.

```
 VPN    PFN    PCID
 0x400  0x9a2  3    <- process A
 0x400  0x177  5    <- process B
```

Linux on x86 assigns each CPU a small pool of PCIDs and recycles them across processes rather than giving every process a permanent tag. PCIDs help reduce **KPTI** overhead (lesson 1). When KPTI is active, a userspace system call switches between reduced user and full kernel page-table views. KPTI also works without PCIDs. With PCIDs, both sets of translations stay cached and the switches cost far less.

Threads in the same process share one address space, so switching between them needs no CR3 write and no flush.

## TLB shootdowns

Each CPU core has its own TLB. Suppose a process has threads on cores 0 to 7 and one thread calls `munmap` (or `mprotect` to remove write access). The kernel updates the page table, but cores 1 to 7 may still hold the old translation.

The kernel must perform a **TLB shootdown**:

1. Update the PTEs.
2. Send an **inter-processor interrupt (IPI)** to every other core that might be running this address space.
3. Each core invalidates the entries (`INVLPG` or a full flush) and acknowledges.
4. The initiating core waits for every acknowledgement before reusing the freed frames.

Shootdown cost varies with hardware, target CPUs and kernel policy. The IPI sequence above is a common implementation, not a requirement that every unmap interrupt every core; deferred invalidation and architectural broadcast mechanisms may differ. Workloads that `mmap` and `munmap` frequently in heavily threaded processes can spend real time here. That is one reason memory allocators avoid returning memory to the OS on every `free`, and why the kernel batches invalidations.

## Huge pages

A 2 MiB page needs one TLB entry for what would otherwise take 512 entries, and its page walk is one level shorter. Both help programs with large working sets.

Linux offers two mechanisms:

| | hugetlbfs | Transparent huge pages |
|---|---|---|
| Setup | Reserve at boot or via `vm.nr_hugepages` | Automatic |
| Sizes | Architecture-dependent; often 2 MiB/1 GiB on x86 | PMD-sized and supported smaller mTHP sizes |
| Swappable | No | Yes |
| Used by | DBs, DPDK, VMs | General apps |

For anonymous THP, `/sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled` is a top-level policy inherited by configured sizes. Modern kernels also have per-size, process and mapping controls. In the simple inherited-policy case:

- `always`: eligible allocations may use THP, subject to size, mapping, process and allocation constraints.
- `madvise`: ordinary automatic allocation is limited to advised eligible regions.
- `never`: disables this automatic policy, but is not an absolute prohibition: `MADV_COLLAPSE` can bypass the sysfs setting, and per-size controls may differ. Use the documented process/mapping controls when full exclusion is required.

The kernel daemon **khugepaged** also scans memory and collapses runs of small pages into huge ones in the background.

### When huge pages hurt

- **Latency spikes.** Finding a free, aligned 2 MiB block may require **compaction** (moving pages around), which can stall an allocation by a workload-dependent amount.
- **Memory bloat.** A program that touches one byte in each of many 2 MiB regions may allocate a 2 MiB page per region instead of a base page, depending on policy and fault type. RSS can grow sharply for sparse workloads.
- **Copy-on-write amplification.** After `fork`, a write fault on a shared huge page can copy a larger unit, split a mapping, or reuse exclusive backing depending on kernel state and policy; it does not invariably copy 2 MiB. Redis forks to write snapshots, which is why the Redis docs advise disabling THP.

Choose THP or explicit HugeTLB based on measured workload and application guidance. PostgreSQL `huge_pages` controls explicit huge pages for its main shared-memory region, not a request for THP. Explicit reservations may fail and require sizing; reserved contiguous pages do not imply fragmentation is impossible elsewhere.

## How the TLB meets the cache

L1 data caches on most x86 cores are **virtually indexed, physically tagged**: the cache set is chosen from address bits inside the page offset (identical in virtual and physical addresses) while the TLB translates the upper bits in parallel. That is why L1 caches are small and many-way associative. The details belong to the Computer Architecture subject.

## Key takeaways
- TLBs cache translations and permissions. A miss can hit another translation-cache level or require a walk; cost depends on the CPU and mapping.
- Locality gives high hit rates for sequential access; random access over large memory can miss constantly.
- EAT = h × hit cost + (1 − h) × miss cost; with deep page tables, even a few per cent of misses is expensive.
- TLB reach = entries × page size; huge pages raise it 512-fold for 2 MiB pages.
- PCIDs and ASIDs tag entries by address space so context switches need not flush; PCIDs make KPTI affordable.
- Mapping removal requires coherent invalidation of stale translations; remote shootdowns commonly use IPIs.
- Huge pages can improve translation reach while adding compaction, memory and COW costs. Follow application-specific guidance and measure the workload.

## Further reading
- [OSTEP: Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs) (PDF)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-tlbs.pdf)
- [Translation lookaside buffer — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Translation_lookaside_buffer)
- [Transparent Hugepage Support — Linux kernel docs](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/mm/transhuge.html)
- [HugeTLB Pages — Linux kernel docs](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/mm/hugetlbpage.html)
- [Diagnosing latency issues (THP section) — Redis docs](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/optimization/latency/)
- [What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory, Ulrich Drepper (PDF)](https://people.freebsd.org/~lstewart/articles/cpumemory.pdf)

questions.prompt: A system has a **single-level** page table. A memory access takes **80 ns**, TLB lookup time is negligible, and the TLB hit rate is **95%**. What is the effective access time?

options.text: 80 ns
options.explanation: This is the cost of a hit only. The 5% of accesses that miss pay for an extra page-table read.

options.text: 84 ns
88 ns
options.explanation: This charges the miss as 80 + 2 × 80. A single-level table needs only one extra read on a miss.

options.text: 160 ns
options.explanation: That is the miss cost, which applies to only 5% of accesses.

questions.workedExample:
1. **Hit**: translation is free, so just the data access: 80 ns.
2. **Miss**: read the PTE from memory (80 ns), then the data (80 ns) = 160 ns.
3. Weight by probability:

```
EAT = 0.95 * 80 + 0.05 * 160
    = 76 + 8
    = 84 ns
```

4. That is a 5% slowdown over no translation at all.

questions.prompt: A loop reads a large array of 8-byte `double`s from start to end. Pages are 4 KiB. Assume a page-aligned array, a cold TLB, one scalar load per element, no translation prefetching and no interfering evictions. In this simplified model, roughly what is the TLB hit rate?

options.text: About 50%
options.explanation: This would only happen if every other access landed on a new page.

options.text: About 99.9%
options.explanation: That is the rate for 4-byte ints (1 miss in 1,024). Doubles are twice as large, so twice as many misses.

options.text: About 0%
options.explanation: That would be the case for a stride of one page or more, not for sequential access.

options.text: About 99.8%
options.explanation: Correct. 4,096 / 8 = 512 doubles per page; the first access to each page misses and the other 511 hit: 511 / 512 ≈ 99.8%.

questions.workedExample: 4,096 / 8 = 512 doubles fit per page. Under the stated model each page gives one miss and 511 hits: 511/512 = 0.998046875, about 99.8%. Real instruction counts, prefetching and translation caches can change observed counters.

questions.prompt: An L1 data TLB holds **64 entries** for 4 KiB pages. What is its TLB reach?

options.text: 64 KiB
options.explanation: This treats each entry as mapping 1 KiB. Each entry maps one whole 4 KiB page.

options.text: 256 KiB
options.explanation: Correct. Reach = entries × page size = 64 × 4 KiB = 256 KiB.

options.text: 4 MiB
options.explanation: That would need 1,024 entries of 4 KiB.

options.text: 128 MiB
options.explanation: That is the reach of 64 entries with 2 MiB huge pages.

questions.workedExample:
TLB reach is the nominal mapped-byte capacity of its entries; conflicts and cold accesses can still miss:

```
reach = entries * page size
      = 64 * 4 KiB = 256 KiB
```

If the hot data is bigger than 256 KiB, the L1 TLB alone cannot cover it, and accesses start falling through to the L2 TLB and then to page walks. With 2 MiB pages, the same 64 entries would cover 64 × 2 MiB = 128 MiB.

questions.prompt: x86-64 with 4-level paging. TLB lookup takes **1 ns**, each memory access takes **100 ns**, there are no page-walk caches, and the TLB hit rate is **98%**. What is the effective access time? Use a serial timing model with 4 KiB pages and no data-cache effects or overlap.

options.text: 101 ns
options.explanation: That is the hit cost alone; the 2% of misses cost five times as much.

options.text: 103 ns
options.explanation: This charges a miss as if the page table had one level (1 + 100 + 100). x86-64 walks four levels.

options.text: 109 ns
501 ns
options.explanation: That is the miss cost, which applies to only 2% of accesses.

questions.workedExample:
1. **Hit**: TLB lookup + data = 1 + 100 = **101 ns**.
2. **Miss**: TLB lookup, then 4 page-table reads, then the data:

```
1 + 4*100 + 100 = 501 ns
```

3. Weighted average:

```
EAT = 0.98*101 + 0.02*501
    = 98.98 + 10.02
    = 109 ns
```

4. Just 2% misses cost about 8% extra. With deeper tables, each miss matters more, which is why page-walk caches and huge pages exist.

questions.prompt: Memory accesses take 100 ns and a TLB miss on this 4-level system costs 500 ns in total (walk plus data). TLB lookup time is negligible. What **minimum TLB hit rate** keeps the effective access time at or below **110 ns**?

options.explanation: At 90%: 0.9 × 100 + 0.1 × 500 = 140 ns, well over the target.

options.text: 98% exactly; anything less exceeds the budget
options.explanation: 98% gives 108 ns, which is within budget, but it is not the minimum. 97.5% gives exactly 110 ns.
That would give 100.4 ns, comfortably within budget, but the question asks for the minimum.

questions.workedExample:
1. Write the EAT as a function of the hit rate `h`:

```
EAT = 100h + 500(1 - h)
    = 500 - 400h
```

2. Require EAT ≤ 110:

```
500 - 400h <= 110
      400h >= 390
         h >= 0.975
```

3. Check: 0.975 × 100 + 0.025 × 500 = 97.5 + 12.5 = 110 ns.

Each percentage point of misses costs 4 ns here, because a miss is 400 ns worse than a hit.

options.text: A has 1,024 times as many TLB misses as B because it makes 1,024 times as many accesses
options.explanation: Most of A's accesses hit pages already in the TLB. Misses depend on new pages touched, not on total accesses.

options.text: B has no TLB misses because it makes so few accesses
options.explanation: B touches 262,144 different pages, far more than the TLB holds, so each access is to a page not in the TLB.

options.text: Both have about 262,144 misses, but A's miss *rate* is about 0.1% while B's is nearly 100%
options.explanation: Correct. Each loop touches every one of the 262,144 pages once. A spreads those misses over 268 million accesses; for B, almost every access is a miss.

options.text: Both have the same miss rate because they touch the same pages
options.explanation: They touch the same pages, so the miss *count* is similar, but B does far fewer accesses per page, so its *rate* is much higher.

questions.workedExample:
1. Pages in the array: 1 GiB / 4 KiB = 262,144.
2. **Loop A**: 2^28 ≈ 268 million accesses. Each page is visited in one burst of 1,024 accesses: 1 miss + 1,023 hits. Misses ≈ 262,144; rate ≈ 1 / 1,024 ≈ 0.1%.
3. **Loop B**: stride 1,024 ints = 4,096 bytes = one page. It makes 262,144 accesses, each on a new page that isn't cached: misses ≈ 262,144; rate ≈ 100%.

These are model miss counts, not a measured PMU prediction. Whether walks dominate latency or huge pages help depends on caches, overlap, CPU and workload.
